title: Week 8: Randomness and simulation
text:
Open in Colab · View on GitHub
Some questions have no formula but can be answered by simulation: build the process in code, run it many times, and look at what happens. Simulation answers “how uncertain is this estimate?”, “what does a shock to a model do to the distribution of outcomes?”, and “does my formula agree with a brute-force check?”
After this week you can:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from pathlib import Path

title: Week 8: Randomness and simulation
text:
1. Random numbers, reproducibly
A computer’s “random” numbers come from a deterministic recipe started at a seed. The same seed gives the same numbers every run, which is what you want in a notebook: your results should not change when someone re-runs it. Create one generator, rng, and draw everything from it.

rng = np.random.default_rng(2027)
print("uniform on [0,1):", rng.random(3).round(3))
print("standard normal:  ", rng.normal(size=3).round(3))
print("dice rolls:       ", rng.integers(1, 7, size=10))
print("pick from a list: ", rng.choice(["low", "mid", "high"], size=5, p=[0.5, 0.3, 0.2]))

rng_a, rng_b = np.random.default_rng(5), np.random.default_rng(5)
print("same seed, same draws:", np.allclose(rng_a.random(4), rng_b.random(4)))

uniform on [0,1): [0.008 0.386 0.083]
standard normal:   [-2.152  1.212 -0.482]
dice rolls:        [4 2 1 4 4 4 1 1 5 1]
pick from a list:  ['low' 'high' 'low' 'high' 'mid']
same seed, same draws: True

title: Week 8: Randomness and simulation
text:
2. The law of large numbers
The average of many independent draws settles down to the true mean. Here, the average of fair-die rolls (true mean 3.5) as the number of rolls grows:

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=10_000)
running = np.cumsum(rolls) / np.arange(1, len(rolls) + 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
ax.plot(running)
ax.axhline(3.5, color="k", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("number of rolls"); ax.set_ylabel("average so far")
ax.set_title("The running average of dice rolls converges to 3.5")
plt.show()
print("average after 10, 100, 10,000 rolls:", running[9].round(2), running[99].round(2), running[-1].round(3))








average after 10, 100, 10,000 rolls: 3.5 3.51 3.501

title: Week 8: Randomness and simulation
section: 3. How wrong is a simulation? The standard error
text:
3. How wrong is a simulation? The standard error
A Monte Carlo estimate is itself random. If \(\hat\mu\) is the average of \(n\) independent draws with standard deviation \(\sigma\), its standard error is \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\): to cut the error in half you need four times the draws.
Example: \(\mathbb{E}[\max(X, Y)]\) for independent standard normals \(X, Y\). The exact answer is \(1/\sqrt{\pi} \approx 0.5642\), so we can check the simulation.

rng = np.random.default_rng(16)
for n in [100, 10_000, 1_000_000]:
    m = np.maximum(rng.normal(size=n), rng.normal(size=n))
    est, se = m.mean(), m.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)
    print(f"n = {n:>9,}: estimate {est:.4f},  standard error {se:.4f},  error vs exact {est - 1/np.sqrt(np.pi):+.4f}")

n =       100: estimate 0.6006,  standard error 0.0832,  error vs exact +0.0365
n =    10,000: estimate 0.5602,  standard error 0.0082,  error vs exact -0.0040
n = 1,000,000: estimate 0.5637,  standard error 0.0008,  error vs exact -0.0005


The errors are about one standard error in size, and the standard error shrinks by a factor of 10 each time \(n\) grows by a factor of 100. Always report the standard error with a Monte Carlo number: without it, nobody knows how many digits to trust.

text:
4. The central limit theorem
Averages of any independent draws with finite variance look normal when \(n\) is large, even if the draws are very skewed. Here, draws from a heavily skewed distribution (exponential), averaged over 50 draws each:

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
single = rng.exponential(size=20_000)
means = rng.exponential(size=(20_000, 50)).mean(axis=1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.3), sharey=False)
axes[0].hist(single, bins=60); axes[0].set_title("single draws (skewed)")
axes[1].hist(means, bins=60); axes[1].set_title("average of 50 draws (nearly normal)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("sd of a single draw:", single.std().round(3), "  sd of the average of 50:", means.std().round(3), "  (1/sqrt(50) =", round(1/np.sqrt(50), 3), ")")








sd of a single draw: 0.989   sd of the average of 50: 0.142   (1/sqrt(50) = 0.141 )

title: Week 8: Randomness and simulation
text:
5. The bootstrap
How uncertain is the average US real GDP growth rate over 1959–2009? There is a formula for the mean, but not for, say, the median or a quantile. The bootstrap needs no formula: resample your own data with replacement many times, recompute the statistic each time, and use the spread of those results as the uncertainty.

DATA = "../data" if Path("../data").exists() else "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WSU-EconS431/site/main/data"
us = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA}/us_macro_1959_2009.csv")
growth = 400 * np.log(us["realgdp"]).diff().dropna().to_numpy()      # annualized quarterly growth, percent
print(f"{len(growth)} quarters; mean {growth.mean():.2f}%, median {np.median(growth):.2f}%")

rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
B = 5000
boot_mean = np.empty(B); boot_med = np.empty(B)
for b in range(B):
    resample = rng.choice(growth, size=len(growth), replace=True)
    boot_mean[b] = resample.mean(); boot_med[b] = np.median(resample)

se_formula = growth.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(growth))
print(f"mean:   bootstrap 95% interval {np.percentile(boot_mean, [2.5, 97.5]).round(2)},  formula {(growth.mean() + np.array([-1.96, 1.96]) * se_formula).round(2)}")
print(f"median: bootstrap 95% interval {np.percentile(boot_med, [2.5, 97.5]).round(2)}   (no simple formula)")

202 quarters; mean 3.10%, median 3.06%
mean:   bootstrap 95% interval [2.62 3.59],  formula [2.62 3.59]
median: bootstrap 95% interval [2.79 3.46]   (no simple formula)


For the mean, the bootstrap and the formula agree, which is the point of checking. For the median there is no easy formula, and the bootstrap gives an interval anyway. One caution: this bootstrap treats quarters as independent draws, which is a simplification for time series (growth in one quarter is not independent of the next), so treat the interval as a rough guide.

title: Week 8: Randomness and simulation
text:
6. Simulating a Markov chain
Last week’s recession chain, with \(P\) estimated from the data. To simulate it, start in a state and at each step draw the next state using the current row of \(P\). Over a long run, the share of time in recession should be close to the stationary distribution we computed last week (about 19%), and the average recession spell should be close to the expected duration (about 4.75 quarters).

P = np.array([[0.9512, 0.0488],
              [0.2105, 0.7895]])
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
T = 20_000
state = np.zeros(T, dtype=int)
for t in range(1, T):
    state[t] = rng.choice(2, p=P[state[t - 1]])

# lengths of the runs of consecutive recession quarters
runs, length = [], 0
for s_ in state:
    if s_ == 1:
        length += 1
    elif length > 0:
        runs.append(length); length = 0
print(f"share of time in recession: {state.mean():.3f}   (stationary distribution: {0.0488 / (0.0488 + 0.2105):.3f})")
print(f"average recession spell: {np.mean(runs):.2f} quarters over {len(runs)} recessions   (formula: {1 / (1 - P[1, 1]):.2f})")

share of time in recession: 0.184   (stationary distribution: 0.188)
average recession spell: 4.57 quarters over 804 recessions   (formula: 4.75)

title: Week 8: Randomness and simulation
text:
7. Random shocks through a model
Week 6’s market (without a tax) has demand \(Q_d = A P^{-\varepsilon}\) and supply \(Q_s = B P^{\gamma}\). Suppose demand is uncertain: \(A = 300\,e^{0.2 z}\) with \(z\) standard normal. What is the distribution of the equilibrium price? We solve the market for each of many draws of \(A\), with brentq (in this simple case there is a formula, \(P = (A/B)^{1/(\varepsilon+\gamma)}\), which lets us check the simulation).

eps, Bs, gam = 1.8, 8, 0.6
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
n = 4000
A_draws = 300 * np.exp(0.2 * rng.normal(size=n))
prices = np.array([brentq(lambda p, A=A: A * p ** (-eps) - Bs * p ** gam, 0.01, 500) for A in A_draws])
formula = (A_draws / Bs) ** (1 / (eps + gam))
print("largest gap between solver and formula:", np.abs(prices - formula).max().round(10))
print(f"mean price {prices.mean():.3f} (price at the average shock: {(300 / Bs) ** (1 / (eps + gam)):.3f}),  5th to 95th percentile: {np.percentile(prices, [5, 95]).round(2)}")
print("share of draws with price above 5:", (prices > 5).mean().round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
ax.hist(prices, bins=50)
ax.axvline(prices.mean(), color="k", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("equilibrium price"); ax.set_title("A 20% demand shock gives a spread of prices")
plt.show()

largest gap between solver and formula: 0.0
mean price 4.547 (price at the average shock: 4.527),  5th to 95th percentile: [3.97 5.19]
share of draws with price above 5: 0.114









A symmetric shock to log demand gives a skewed distribution of prices (the mean is slightly above the price at the average shock), and the question “how likely is a price above 5?” has an answer that no point forecast can give. That is what simulation is for.

title: Week 6: Root-finding and optimization
text:
Open in Colab · View on GitHub
Most economic models have an equilibrium that solves an equation or a choice that maximizes an objective, and most realistic versions have no tidy formula. In Week 2 you wrote bisection to solve an equation by repeatedly halving a bracket, and in Week 3 you searched a grid for a maximum. This week you use SciPy’s professional versions of both, and learn what to check afterward.
After this week you can:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import brentq, root_scalar, root, minimize_scalar, minimize
from scipy.integrate import quad

title: Week 6: Root-finding and optimization
text:
1. An equilibrium with a tax
Demand is \(Q_d = A\,P^{-\varepsilon}\), which has constant elasticity \(-\varepsilon\). Supply is \(Q_s = B\,(P - t)^{\gamma}\) for a per-unit tax \(t\) on sellers: sellers keep \(P - t\). With no tax there is a formula, \(P^* = (A/B)^{1/(\varepsilon + \gamma)}\), which we use to check our answers. With a tax, there is no formula, so we solve \(Q_d(P) = Q_s(P)\) numerically.

A, eps, B, gamma = 200, 1.5, 5, 0.8

def demand(p):
    return A * p ** (-eps)

def supply(p, t=0):
    """Quantity supplied when buyers pay p and sellers keep p - t."""
    return B * np.maximum(p - t, 0) ** gamma

def excess(p, t=0):
    """Excess demand. The equilibrium price is where this is zero."""
    return demand(p) - supply(p, t)

p_formula = (A / B) ** (1 / (eps + gamma))
print(f"no-tax equilibrium from the formula: P* = {p_formula:.4f}, Q* = {demand(p_formula):.3f}")

no-tax equilibrium from the formula: P* = 4.9722, Q* = 18.039


brentq(f, a, b) finds a zero of f between a and b. Like bisection it needs a bracket: f(a) and f(b) must have opposite signs. Excess demand is positive at a low price and negative at a high price, so any wide bracket works.

print(excess(0.5), excess(100))           # positive, then negative: the bracket is valid
p_star = brentq(excess, 0.5, 100)
print(f"brentq: P* = {p_star:.6f}")

562.8136790617455 -198.85358527674867
brentq: P* = 4.972191


Always check the answer. Here we can compare with the formula, and in general you check that the function really is close to zero at the answer (the residual):

print("residual:", excess(p_star))
assert np.isclose(p_star, p_formula)

residual: 0.0


root_scalar is the same solver with a report on what happened. Compare the work with your Week 2 bisection (which halves the bracket every time):

def bisect_count(f, lo, hi, tol=1e-12):
    n = 0
    while hi - lo > tol:
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        if f(lo) * f(mid) <= 0:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid
        n += 1
    return (lo + hi) / 2, n

res = root_scalar(excess, bracket=[0.5, 100], method="brentq")
print(f"brentq:   root {res.root:.8f}, {res.iterations} iterations, converged: {res.converged}")
p_bis, n_bis = bisect_count(excess, 0.5, 100)
print(f"bisection: root {p_bis:.8f}, {n_bis} iterations")

brentq:   root 4.97219122, 11 iterations, converged: True
bisection: root 4.97219122, 47 iterations


Brent’s method combines bisection’s safety with faster steps when the function is smooth, so it needs far fewer evaluations. Both need a sign change; without one they stop with an error rather than a wrong answer:

brentq(excess, 10, 100)       # excess demand is negative at both ends: no bracket

title: Week 6: Root-finding and optimization
text:
2. Passing parameters with args
The solver calls f(x) with one number, but our excess also needs the tax. Pass extra arguments with args=(...), or wrap the function in a lambda. Now solve for a tax of 2 per unit. The lowest price sellers will accept is \(t\), so the bracket starts just above \(t\):

t = 2
res = root_scalar(excess, args=(t,), bracket=[t + 1e-6, 200], method="brentq")
p_c = res.root              # price buyers pay
p_s = p_c - t               # price sellers keep
q_t = demand(p_c)
print(f"buyers pay {p_c:.3f}, sellers keep {p_s:.3f}, quantity {q_t:.3f} (was {demand(p_formula):.3f})")
print(f"consumers bear {(p_c - p_formula) / t:.0%} of the tax, sellers {(p_formula - p_s) / t:.0%}")
print("residual:", excess(p_c, t))

buyers pay 5.766, sellers keep 3.766, quantity 14.444 (was 18.039)
consumers bear 40% of the tax, sellers 60%
residual: 0.0


The tax raises the price buyers pay by less than the tax and lowers the price sellers keep, so the burden is shared; with these elasticities consumers bear about 40%. (Week 10 explains why the split depends on the elasticities.) Putting the solve in a function lets us study many tax rates:

def solve_market(t):
    """Equilibrium price buyers pay when the tax is t."""
    return root_scalar(excess, args=(t,), bracket=[t + 1e-6, 200], method="brentq").root

taxes = np.linspace(0, 10, 41)
p_buy = np.array([solve_market(t) for t in taxes])
q_eq = demand(p_buy)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
ax1.plot(taxes, p_buy, label="price buyers pay")
ax1.plot(taxes, p_buy - taxes, label="price sellers keep")
ax1.set_xlabel("Tax per unit")
ax1.set_ylabel("Price")
ax1.legend()
ax2.plot(taxes, taxes * q_eq, color="tab:green")
ax2.set_xlabel("Tax per unit")
ax2.set_ylabel("Tax revenue")
ax2.set_title("Revenue rises, then falls")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Week 6: Root-finding and optimization
text:
3. Systems of equations: root
When two markets interact, you solve for two prices at once. Let coffee (price \(p_1\)) and tea (\(p_2\)) be substitutes: demand for each falls with its own price and rises with the other’s. The function returns the vector of excess demands, and root finds the vector of prices where both are zero from a starting guess x0.

def excess_two(p):
    p1, p2 = p
    ed1 = 100 * p1 ** -1.2 * p2 ** 0.3 - 4 * p1       # demand minus supply, market 1
    ed2 = 80 * p2 ** -1.0 * p1 ** 0.2 - 6 * p2        # demand minus supply, market 2
    return [ed1, ed2]

sol = root(excess_two, x0=[5.0, 5.0])
print("success:", sol.success, " prices:", sol.x.round(4))
print("residuals:", np.array(excess_two(sol.x)).round(10))

success: True  prices: [5.272  4.3119]
residuals: [-2.e-10 -0.e+00]


A system has no bracket, so root needs a starting guess. Try other starting guesses; if different ones give different answers, or success is False, investigate before trusting any of them.

title: Week 6: Root-finding and optimization
text:
4. Optimization: minimize_scalar
SciPy only minimizes, so to maximize profit you minimize minus profit. A monopolist faces inverse demand \(P = a - bq\) and cost \(C(q) = F + cq + dq^2/2\). Profit is \(\pi(q) = (a - bq)q - C(q)\) and calculus gives \(q^* = (a - c)/(2b + d)\), which we use to check the solver.

a, b, c, d, F = 100, 2, 10, 1, 50

def profit(q):
    return (a - b * q) * q - (F + c * q + d * q ** 2 / 2)

res = minimize_scalar(lambda q: -profit(q), bounds=(0, a / b), method="bounded")
print(f"solver: q = {res.x:.4f}, profit = {-res.fun:.3f}, success: {res.success}")
print(f"calculus: q = {(a - c) / (2 * b + d):.4f}")

solver: q = 18.0000, profit = 760.000, success: True
calculus: q = 18.0000


bounds=(0, a/b) keeps the search where the model makes sense (quantity between 0 and the choke quantity), and method="bounded" is the scalar method that respects them. Because the optimizer works on whatever function you give it, the same code solves the problem when cost is complicated and calculus is messy.
Optimizers can be nested. A government that wants to maximize tax revenue chooses \(t\) to maximize \(t \cdot Q(t)\), where \(Q(t)\) comes from solving the market (Section 2). The inner solve runs inside the objective:

def revenue(t):
    return t * demand(solve_market(t))

res = minimize_scalar(lambda t: -revenue(t), bounds=(0, 10), method="bounded")
print(f"revenue-maximizing tax: {res.x:.3f}, revenue {-res.fun:.2f}, success: {res.success}")

revenue-maximizing tax: 8.229, revenue 54.81, success: True


That agrees with the right-hand figure in Section 2, where revenue peaks at a tax a little above 8 and then falls as the tax shrinks the market.

title: Week 6: Root-finding and optimization
text:
5. A constrained choice: minimize
A consumer with income \(m\) buys \(x\) and \(y\) at prices \(p_x\) and \(p_y\) to maximize Cobb–Douglas utility \(u = x^{\alpha} y^{1-\alpha}\) subject to the budget \(p_x x + p_y y = m\). The solution has a formula, \(x^* = \alpha m/p_x\) and \(y^* = (1-\alpha)m/p_y\), so we can check the solver, but the code below works for any utility function.

alpha, px, py, m = 0.4, 2.0, 5.0, 100.0

def utility(z):
    x, y = z
    return x ** alpha * y ** (1 - alpha)

budget = {"type": "eq", "fun": lambda z: m - px * z[0] - py * z[1]}      # equals zero when the budget is spent

res = minimize(lambda z: -utility(z), x0=[10.0, 5.0], bounds=[(1e-9, None), (1e-9, None)],
               constraints=[budget], method="SLSQP")
print("success:", res.success, " x, y =", res.x.round(4), " utility =", round(-res.fun, 4))
print("formula:", alpha * m / px, (1 - alpha) * m / py)

success: True  x, y = [20. 12.]  utility = 14.7204
formula: 20.0 12.0


x0 is a starting guess, bounds keeps both goods positive (the logarithm and powers misbehave at zero), and the constraint dictionary says the budget holds with equality.

title: Week 6: Root-finding and optimization
text:
6. Areas under curves: quad
Consumer surplus is the area between the demand curve and the price, from 0 to the quantity bought: \(CS = \int_0^{Q}\bigl(P_d(q) - p\bigr)\,dq\), where \(P_d(q) = (A/q)^{1/\varepsilon}\) is the inverse demand. quad(f, a, b) integrates numerically and returns the area and an error estimate. Producer surplus is the area between the price sellers keep and the supply curve \(P_s(q) = (q/B)^{1/\gamma}\).

P_d = lambda q: (A / q) ** (1 / eps)         # inverse demand
P_s = lambda q: (q / B) ** (1 / gamma)       # inverse supply

def welfare(p_buy, p_sell, q):
    cs = quad(lambda x: P_d(x) - p_buy, 0, q)[0]
    ps = quad(lambda x: p_sell - P_s(x), 0, q)[0]
    return cs, ps

q0 = demand(p_formula)
cs0, ps0 = welfare(p_formula, p_formula, q0)
cs_formula = A ** (1 / eps) * q0 ** (1 - 1 / eps) / (1 - 1 / eps) - p_formula * q0      # integral by hand
print(f"no tax:  CS = {cs0:.2f} (by hand {cs_formula:.2f}), PS = {ps0:.2f}")

cs1, ps1 = welfare(p_c, p_s, q_t)
revenue_2 = t * q_t
dwl = (cs0 + ps0) - (cs1 + ps1 + revenue_2)
print(f"tax of {t}: CS = {cs1:.2f}, PS = {ps1:.2f}, revenue = {revenue_2:.2f}, deadweight loss = {dwl:.2f}")

no tax:  CS = 179.38 (by hand 179.38), PS = 49.83
tax of 2: CS = 166.58, PS = 30.22, revenue = 28.89, deadweight loss = 3.53


The tax transfers some surplus to the government as revenue and destroys the rest of the loss: the deadweight loss. You’ll use this calculation again in Module 4.

title: Week 6: Root-finding and optimization
text:
7. When solvers fail
Local optima. An optimizer follows the function uphill (or downhill) from the starting guess and stops at the first peak it reaches. If the function has several peaks, different starts give different answers:

def f(x):
    return np.sin(3 * x) + 0.5 * x - 0.05 * x ** 2      # a function with several peaks

for x0 in [-4, -1, 0.5, 3]:
    r = minimize(lambda z: -f(z[0]), [x0])
    print(f"start {x0:>4}: peak at x = {r.x[0]:6.3f}, f = {-r.fun:.3f}")

xs = np.linspace(-5, 5, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.3))
ax.plot(xs, f(xs))
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("f(x)")
ax.set_title("Four starting points find four different peaks")
plt.show()

start   -4: peak at x = -3.569, f = -1.463
start   -1: peak at x = -1.498, f = 0.115
start  0.5: peak at x =  0.573, f = 1.259
start    3: peak at x =  2.644, f = 1.969









Only one of those peaks is the global maximum. The usual defense is to try several starting guesses (or a coarse grid search first, as in Week 3) and keep the best, and to plot the function when you can.
A checklist after any solver call:

Did it report success? (res.success, res.converged, res.message)
Is the residual (or the first-order condition) close to zero at the answer?
Does the answer make economic sense (positive price, quantity within bounds)?
Does a closed form, a grid search, or another starting guess give the same answer?
Is the answer at a bound? That means the bound, not the optimizer, chose it.

The four basic types are float (decimal numbers), int (whole numbers), str (text), and bool (True/False). Multiplying a float by an int gives a float.
Because the right side is computed first, a name can appear on both sides:

quantity = quantity + 5   # take the old value, add 5, store the result under the same name
quantity += 5             # shorthand for the same thing
quantity

50


Floats are approximations. Computers store most decimals in binary, so tiny rounding errors appear. Never test two floats for exact equality; check whether they are within a tolerance. Every numerical solver in this course stops at a tolerance for the same reason.

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 1e-12)

False
0.30000000000000004
True



Lists and dictionaries
A list holds values in order; positions start at 0. A dictionary stores values under names, which is a convenient way to keep a model’s parameters together.

prices = [2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5]
print(prices[0], prices[-1], len(prices))   # first, last, how many

params = {"a": 100, "b": 2, "c": 10, "d": 1}
print(params["a"], params["d"])

2.0 3.5 4
100 1




Printing readably
An f-string (a string starting with f) puts values inside text. The part after : controls the format: .2f means two decimals, , adds thousands separators.

print(f"{firm} earns ${price * quantity:,.2f} selling {quantity} units.")

A price ceiling matters only if it is set below the equilibrium price. Code makes that decision with if:

p_star = 30      # equilibrium price from Week 1
ceiling = 25

if ceiling < p_star:
    print(f"The ceiling binds: price is held at {ceiling}.")
else:
    print(f"The ceiling does not bind: price stays at {p_star}.")

The ceiling binds: price is held at 25.


Indentation is part of the code. The indented lines belong to the if or the else. The editor indents four spaces for you after a colon.

Use elif (“else if”) for more than two cases. Here we classify a price elasticity of demand:

e = -0.6

if abs(e) > 1:
    label = "elastic"
elif abs(e) < 1:
    label = "inelastic"

text:
3. Repeating work: for loops
A for loop runs the indented block once for each item in a sequence. With linear demand \(Q = a - bP\):

a, b = 100, 2

for p in [10, 20, 30, 40]:
    q = a - b * p
    print(f"P = {p:>3}:  Q = {q:>4},  revenue = {p * q:>5}")

P =  10:  Q =   80,  revenue =   800
P =  20:  Q =   60,  revenue =  1200
P =  30:  Q =   40,  revenue =  1200
P =  40:  Q =   20,  revenue =   800


range(start, stop) produces whole numbers from start up to, but not including, stop. A common pattern is to keep track of the best value found so far. This loop finds the revenue-maximizing whole-number price:

best_p, best_rev = None, -1

for p in range(0, 51):          # 0, 1, ..., 50
    rev = p * (a - b * p)
    if rev > best_rev:
        best_p, best_rev = p, rev

print(f"Revenue is highest at P = {best_p}, where it equals {best_rev}.")

Revenue is highest at P = 25, where it equals 1250.


Check it with calculus: revenue \(R = P(a - bP)\) has \(dR/dP = a - 2bP = 0\) at \(P = a/(2b) = 25\). The loop and the derivative agree. When a model has no closed-form answer, the loop still works; that is the main reason to compute.
A list comprehension builds a list from a loop in one line:

revenues = [p * (a - b * p) for p in range(0, 51)]
print(max(revenues), revenues.index(max(revenues)))   # largest value, and its position

4. Repeating until done: while loops
A while loop keeps going as long as its condition is true. Use it when you don’t know in advance how many steps you need. How many years until savings double at 5% interest?

balance, years = 1.0, 0
rate = 0.05

while balance < 2:
    balance = balance * (1 + rate)
    years += 1

print(f"{years} years (the rule of 70 says about {70 / (rate * 100):.0f})")

15 years (the rule of 70 says about 14)


Make sure something inside the loop moves you toward ending it. If a cell runs forever, press the Interrupt (square stop) button at the top of the notebook, fix the loop, and rerun.

title: Week 2: Python fundamentals I
text:
5. Functions
A function gives a calculation a name, takes inputs (parameters), and hands back a result with return. Once written and tested, it can be reused with any inputs.

def revenue(p, a, b):
    """Total revenue at price p when demand is Q = a - b*p."""
    return p * (a - b * p)

print(revenue(25, 100, 2))
print(revenue(25, a=120, b=3))     # arguments can be passed by name

1250
1125


The text in triple quotes is a docstring. It says what the function does; hover over the function name in the editor to see it.
return is not print. A function that only prints shows a number but gives back nothing (None), so you can’t use its result in later calculations:

def revenue_printed(p, a, b):
    print(p * (a - b * p))

x = revenue_printed(25, 100, 2)
print("x is", x)

1250
x is None


Default values let you leave out arguments that rarely change. This cost function has a fixed cost and a quadratic variable cost, \(C(q) = F + cq^2\):

def cost(q, fixed=200, c=0.5):
    """Total cost of producing q units."""
    return fixed + c * q**2

print(cost(10), cost(10, fixed=0), cost(10, c=1))

250.0 50.0 300


Pass what a function needs as arguments. Names created inside a function exist only inside it, and a function that quietly reads variables defined elsewhere in the notebook breaks when those change. That is why the PS02 functions take a and b as inputs.

section: 6. Putting it together: solving an equation by bisection
text:
6. Putting it together: solving an equation by bisection
A firm sells at price \(p = 40\) with cost \(C(q) = 200 + 0.5q^2\). Profit is \(\pi(q) = pq - C(q)\). What is the smallest quantity at which the firm breaks even (\(\pi(q) = 0\))?
Bisection needs only one fact: if profit is negative at lo and positive at hi, the break-even point lies between them. Check the midpoint, keep the half that still brackets the answer, and repeat until the bracket is tiny.

def profit(q, p=40, fixed=200, c=0.5):
    """Profit at quantity q."""
    return p * q - cost(q, fixed, c)

print(profit(0), profit(20))   # negative, then positive: the answer is between 0 and 20

-200.0 400.0



lo, hi = 0.0, 20.0
tol = 1e-8
steps = 0

while hi - lo > tol:
    mid = (lo + hi) / 2
    if profit(mid) < 0:   # still losing money at mid: break-even is to the right
        lo = mid
    else:                 # making money at mid: break-even is to the left
        hi = mid
    steps += 1

q_be = (lo + hi) / 2
print(f"Break-even at q = {q_be:.6f} after {steps} halvings")

Break-even at q = 5.358984 after 31 halvings


Check against the quadratic formula: \(0.5q^2 - 40q + 200 = 0\) gives \(q = 40 - \sqrt{1200} \approx 5.358984\). Each halving cuts the bracket in two, so 31 steps shrink a width of 20 below \(10^{-8}\).
The if above works because profit rises on this bracket. A general version compares signs instead, so it works whichever way the function slopes. Functions can take other functions as inputs:

def bisect(f, lo, hi, tol=1e-8):
    """Return x in [lo, hi] with f(x) close to 0. f(lo) and f(hi) must differ in sign."""
    if f(lo) * f(hi) > 0:
        raise ValueError("f(lo) and f(hi) must have opposite signs")
    while hi - lo > tol:
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        if f(lo) * f(mid) <= 0:   # sign change in the left half
            hi = mid
        else:                     # sign change in the right half
            lo = mid
    return (lo + hi) / 2

print(bisect(profit, 0, 20))     # first break-even point
print(bisect(profit, 20, 100))   # profit turns negative again at high output

5.3589838510379195
74.64101614896208


In Week 6 you’ll use scipy.optimize.brentq, which does the same job in fewer steps. Now you know what’s inside it. PS02 asks you to adapt this idea to find a market equilibrium.

7. Debugging
Errors are normal; reading them is a skill. When a cell fails, Python prints a traceback:

Read the last line first. It names the error type and gives a message.
Find the arrow (---->). It points to the line that failed.
Fix that line, or the line that gave it a bad value, and rerun.

Each cell below fails on purpose. If you use Run All, it may stop at the first one; run the rest of the notebook a cell at a time.

revnue(25, 100, 2)


---------------------------------------------------------------------------
NameError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[18], line 1
----> 1 revnue(25, 100, 2)

NameError: name 'revnue' is not defined



NameError: Python doesn’t know the name revnue. Usually a typo, or a cell defining the name hasn’t been run yet (run cells from the top).

revenue(25, 100)


---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[19], line 1
----> 1 revenue(25, 100)

TypeError: revenue() missing 1 required positional argument: 'b'



TypeError: the function needs three arguments and got two.







Error
Usual cause




NameError
typo, or the defining cell wasn’t run


TypeError
wrong number or kind of arguments, e.g. adding text to a number


SyntaxError, IndentationError
missing colon, bracket, or quote; inconsistent indentation


ZeroDivisionError
dividing by zero, often at a corner of a model, such as zero quantity


IndexError, KeyError
asking a list for a position it doesn’t have, or a dictionary for a missing name




Bugs that don’t raise errors
The most dangerous bugs produce a number that looks fine. This demand function has the wrong sign and runs without complaint:

def demand_buggy(p, a, b):
    """Quantity demanded at price p."""
    return a + b * p    # should be a - b*p

demand_buggy(10, 100, 2)

120


The defense is to test a case you can do in your head. An assert stops with an error if its condition is false, so a wrong function can’t slip by. PS self-check cells work this way.

assert demand_buggy(0, 100, 2) == 100              # passes: at P = 0 the sign doesn't matter
assert demand_buggy(10, 100, 2) == 80, "demand should fall as price rises"


---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AssertionError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[21], line 2
      1 assert demand_buggy(0, 100, 2) == 100              # passes: at P = 0 the sign doesn't matter
----> 2 assert demand_buggy(10, 100, 2) == 80, "demand should fall as price rises"

AssertionError: demand should fall as price rises





Using an AI chat assistant to debug
Through Week 5, chat assistants are allowed and inline autocomplete stays off (see Policies). A chat assistant is most useful when you ask it to explain rather than to fix:

Paste the whole traceback and the cell that failed.
Say what you expected to happen.
Ask: “Explain what this error means and where my reasoning went wrong. Don’t rewrite my code.”
Make the change yourself, rerun, and check a case you know the answer to.
Record what you asked and how you checked it in the AI usage note.

Assistants are often confidently wrong about economics even when the code runs. Step 4 is the part that protects your grade.

title: Work on your own computer (optional)
text:
Steps

Git: version-control software. It saves snapshots (“commits”) of your work and syncs them with your private course repo on GitHub. You’ll use it to get each new problem set (pull) and to hand in your work (commit and push), mostly through buttons in Positron. You’ll type Git commands in Positron’s terminal only during setup and for the occasional fix.

Windows: install “Git for Windows” from git-scm.com and accept every default. It includes the sign-in helper Git needs for GitHub.
Mac: open Terminal, type git --version, and accept the prompt to install the Command Line Tools. Then install the GitHub CLI from cli.github.com and run gh auth login (choose the web-browser login) and gh auth setup-git, so Git can sign in to GitHub.

Positron (free, from Posit): the program where you’ll do all your coding. It opens your course repo, runs Python notebooks and scripts, shows your data and plots, and has Git built in. Download and install it from positron.posit.co.

When you first open your course folder, Positron asks whether you trust the authors of the files. Click Yes, I trust the authors; it’s your own repo.
If Positron offers to create a Python environment, decline. Step 6 builds the course environment instead.
If Positron asks “Would you like Positron to periodically run git fetch?”, click Yes. It checks GitHub for new problem sets without changing your files; a small down-arrow count in the status bar means something new is ready to pull.
The first time you commit, Positron may ask whether to stage all your changes and commit them directly. Click Yes (or Always).
The first time you click Sync Changes, Positron asks you to confirm pulling and pushing. Click OK (or OK, Don’t Ask Again).
If Positron asks you to sign in to GitHub, your browser will show “Authorize Visual-Studio-Code”. That’s expected: Positron is built on VS Code. If Positron then says sign-in failed, see the Setup FAQ.
If Positron offers to turn on an AI assistant or code completions, skip it for now. AI autocomplete stays off through Week 5 (see Policies).

uv: a free tool that installs Python and the course packages, so everyone’s setup is identical. To install it, open a terminal: in Positron, choose Terminal > New Terminal (on Windows this opens PowerShell; on a Mac, a regular terminal). Then paste the command for your system and press Enter:

Windows:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
Mac:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
Not using Positron’s terminal? On Windows, click Start, type PowerShell, and open Windows PowerShell. On a Mac, press Cmd+Space, type Terminal, and press Return.
When it finishes, quit and reopen Positron (or close and reopen the terminal) so it can find uv. Check with uv --version, which should print a version number.

Tell Git who you are. In a terminal, paste each command, replace the text in quotes with your own name and the email on your GitHub account, then press Enter:
git config --global user.name "First Last"
git config --global user.email "your-github-email@example.com"
Clone your repo. Make a folder such as EconS431 directly in your home folder (C:\Users\<you>\EconS431 or /Users/<you>/EconS431). Not in OneDrive, Dropbox, or iCloud, and not on your Desktop or in Documents, which many laptops sync automatically. Then, in a Positron terminal:
cd ~/EconS431
git clone https://github.com/WSU-EconS431/2027sp-<your-username>.git
The first clone opens a GitHub sign-in window; choose the browser option. Then open the new folder: File > Open Folder > EconS431/2027sp-<your-username>.
Build the environment. In a Positron terminal inside your repo, run uv sync. Then click the interpreter name at the top right and choose the Python from .venv (labeled econs431). If Positron offers to create an environment, decline: uv sync builds the course one.
Check it. Run uv run python check_setup.py. Every line should start with [OK]. Then open ps01/ps01.ipynb, choose the same econs431 kernel at the top right of the notebook, complete it, commit, push, and submit the commit link in Canvas.

My repo is greyed out, or I don’t see “Create codespace”

Your repo’s page > Code > Codespaces tab > click the codespace listed there (it has a random two-word name). You can also see all of yours at github.com/codespaces. Reuse that one codespace all semester rather than creating new ones.


A notebook says “No module named numpy” (or asks me to select a kernel)
Python reports a missing package as ModuleNotFoundError: No module named ....

Check the kernel. Click Select Kernel (or the kernel name) at the top right of the notebook, choose Python Environments, and pick the one in .venv. Then run the cells again. This fixes it almost every time.
Still missing? Run uv sync. Open a terminal, a window for typing commands to the computer: click the ☰ menu at the top left, then Terminal > New Terminal. Working on your own computer? See the Positron version.


I pressed Ctrl+W (or another shortcut) and my browser tab closed

Will I run out of codespace time?
Unlikely if you stop your codespace when you’re done. Your account includes about 60 hours a month, or 90 with GitHub student benefits. Check your usage under Settings > Billing on GitHub. If you’re about to run out, set up your own computer as a backup.


My codespace disappeared
A codespace you don’t open for several weeks is deleted, along with anything not pushed to GitHub. Create a new one from your repo page; everything you pushed is still there. This is why every work session ends with commit and push.


“Pull” fails after I worked in a codespace and on my laptop
Your two copies changed in different ways. Always pull when you sit down and push when you get up. If a pull still fails, don’t force anything; post the message on Discussions.

I see two Pythons, or Python 3.14, or a Python I don’t recognize

Your own computer: the Python environment

Positron shows a red ✕ and “A dedicated Python environment is available” (or offers to “Create Python environment”)
Don’t click the create button. It builds a different environment from the course one. Instead:

Open your repo folder (File > Open Folder). It’s the folder that contains pyproject.toml.
Open a terminal (Terminal > New Terminal) and run uv sync.
Click the interpreter name at the top right of Positron and choose the Python from .venv.



A command gives “No module named uv” (or a Python SyntaxError)
You typed it into the Console, the panel with the >>> prompt, which runs Python code only. Commands such as uv, git, and cd go in the Terminal (Terminal > New Terminal), whose prompt shows your folder, like PS C:\Users\<you>\EconS431\2027sp-<your-username>>.


uv sync says it can’t find pyproject.toml
The terminal is in the wrong folder. Open your repo folder in Positron (File > Open Folder), then open a new terminal; it starts in the right place.


uv sync fails with “Failed to hardlink files” or “os error 396”
A sync or backup tool (OneDrive, Dropbox, and others) is blocking the file links uv uses to save disk space. Tell uv to copy instead:
uv sync --link-mode=copy
Current course repos already include this setting, so it should only affect older copies.


A notebook says “No module named numpy” (or pandas, scipy, …)
The notebook is probably running a different Python from the course one. Click the kernel name at the top right of the notebook and choose the Python from .venv (it’s labeled econs431). Then Restart the kernel and run the cells again. Positron usually remembers this choice for the folder.
If the package is still missing, open a terminal (Terminal > New Terminal) with your course repo folder open in Positron, run uv sync, then restart the kernel again.


check_setup.py says “Repo is outside a cloud-synced folder” is a problem
Your repo is inside OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud, or Google Drive. Syncing the .venv folder (about 850 MB and 25,000 files) causes slowdowns and locked-file errors. Move the repo to a folder in your home folder that doesn’t sync, such as C:\Users\<you>\EconS431 (Windows) or /Users/<you>/EconS431 (Mac).
Watch out: on many laptops, Desktop and Documents are synced (OneDrive on Windows, iCloud on Mac) even if you never set that up. If the path contains OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud, or Mobile Documents, it syncs.


My .venv folder is huge, and Windows won’t let me delete or move it
Its size is normal: it holds compiled scientific libraries. It’s never uploaded to GitHub, and uv sync rebuilds it in a minute, so deleting it is always safe.
Windows refuses because a program still has its files open:

Quit Positron completely, including from the system tray.
In Task Manager, end any leftover python.exe processes.
If the folder is in OneDrive or Dropbox, pause syncing.
Delete it. If Windows still refuses, restart the computer and delete it before opening anything else.

Spaces just inside the dollar signs. Write $P^*$, not $ P^* $. Some editors forgive the spaces; the course website doesn’t.
Blank lines inside display math. Everything between the opening $$ and the closing $$ must be one block with no empty lines.
Unmatched braces or misspelled commands, such as \frac{a}{b or \aplha. The equation shows up as raw text or a red error message. Read it like a traceback: find the first brace or command that doesn’t match.

3. Indexing, slicing, and Boolean masks
Positions work as in lists, starting at 0. A slice start:stop:step takes a range of positions (again excluding stop).

text:
4. Functions that work on arrays
A function built from arithmetic works on arrays with no changes. This is the Week 2 style of function, now applied to a whole grid:

def demand(p, a, b):
    """Quantity demanded at price p (a number or an array)."""
    return a - b * p

demand(np.array([0, 30, 60, 75]), a, b)

array([ 90. ,  45. ,   0. , -22.5])


Look at the last value: \(P = 75\) is above the choke price \(a/b = 60\), and linear demand turns negative there. A Week 2 if can’t fix that for arrays, because if needs one True or False, and a comparison on an array gives many:

def demand_nonneg_loop_style(p, a, b):
    if p > a / b:
        return 0
    return a - b * p

demand_nonneg_loop_style(grid, a, b)

title: Week 3: NumPy arrays, vectorization, and plotting
text:
5. How much faster?
Vectorized code runs as compiled loops inside NumPy instead of one Python step at a time. Compare total revenue over a million prices:

import time

p_big = np.linspace(0, 60, 1_000_000)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
total = 0.0
for p_i in p_big:
    total += p_i * (a - b * p_i)
t_loop = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
total_vec = np.sum(p_big * (a - b * p_big))
t_vec = time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f"loop:       {t_loop:.3f} s")
print(f"vectorized: {t_vec:.4f} s  ({t_loop / t_vec:.0f}x faster)")
print("same answer:", np.isclose(total, total_vec))

loop:       0.565 s
vectorized: 0.0135 s  (42x faster)
same answer: True


Speed matters once you simulate many agents or solve a model thousands of times (Weeks 8 and 15). Until then, the bigger gain is that the vectorized line is shorter and matches the math.

text:
6. Searching a grid
Summaries collapse an array to one number: np.sum, np.mean, np.max, np.min. The arg versions, np.argmax and np.argmin, give the position of the largest or smallest element, which you then use to look up the price.
Revenue-maximizing price. Last week this took a loop and an if. Now:

p_fine = np.linspace(0, 60, 6001)              # steps of 0.01
rev = p_fine * demand(p_fine, a, b)
i = np.argmax(rev)
print(f"best price {p_fine[i]:.2f}, revenue {rev[i]:.2f}   (calculus: a/(2b) = {a / (2 * b):.2f})")

best price 30.00, revenue 1350.00   (calculus: a/(2b) = 30.00)


Equilibrium on a grid. The equilibrium is where excess demand is closest to zero:

ed = demand(p_fine, a, b) - (c + d * p_fine)
j = np.argmin(np.abs(ed))
p_star, q_star = p_fine[j], demand(p_fine[j], a, b)
print(f"grid: P* = {p_star:.2f}, Q* = {q_star:.2f}   formula: P* = {(a - c) / (b + d):.2f}")

grid: P* = 20.00, Q* = 60.00   formula: P* = 20.00


The equilibrium price (20) is not the revenue-maximizing price (30). A competitive market doesn’t maximize sellers’ revenue; no single seller controls the price. Week 11 returns to this with monopoly.
A grid answer is only as precise as the grid’s step. Bisection (Week 2) and SciPy’s solvers (Week 6) home in on the exact value instead.
Comparative statics without a loop. Week 1 looped over demand intercepts. Arrays do the whole set at once:

a_values = np.arange(60, 121, 10)
p_stars = (a_values - c) / (b + d)
q_stars = a_values - b * p_stars

7. Plotting with Matplotlib
Every figure in this course starts the same way: fig, ax = plt.subplots() creates a figure and a set of axes, and you draw on ax. Economists put price on the vertical axis, so quantity goes first in ax.plot(x, y).

p_plot = np.linspace(0, 60, 200)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.plot(demand(p_plot, a, b), p_plot, label="Demand")
ax.plot(c + d * p_plot, p_plot, label="Supply")
ax.plot(q_star, p_star, "o", color="black")
ax.annotate(f"  equilibrium ({q_star:.0f}, {p_star:.0f})", (q_star, p_star))

# Shade consumer surplus: between the demand curve and P*, from Q = 0 to Q*
q_cs = np.linspace(0, q_star, 100)
ax.fill_between(q_cs, (a - q_cs) / b, p_star, alpha=0.3, label="Consumer surplus")

ax.set_xlabel("Quantity (units per week)")
ax.set_ylabel("Price ($ per unit)")
ax.set_title("Competitive market")
ax.set_xlim(0, 95)
ax.set_ylim(0, 62)
ax.legend()
plt.show()








The shading uses inverse demand, \(P = (a - Q)/b\), because the vertical axis is price.
Several panels. plt.subplots(1, 2) returns two axes side by side:

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
ax1.plot(a_values, p_stars, "o-")
ax1.set_xlabel("Demand intercept a")
ax1.set_ylabel("Equilibrium price")
ax2.plot(a_values, q_stars, "o-", color="tab:orange")
ax2.set_xlabel("Demand intercept a")
ax2.set_ylabel("Equilibrium quantity")
fig.suptitle("Stronger demand raises both price and quantity")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








To save a figure next to your notebook for a report or slide, add fig.savefig("market.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") before plt.show().
Checklist for a figure someone else will read

Axis labels say what is measured, with units.
A legend whenever there is more than one line.
The title states the takeaway, not just the variables.
Axis ranges show the interesting part; don’t let a negative quantity stretch the plot.
Matplotlib’s default colors are colorblind-safe. If you choose your own, check them.

title: Week 3: NumPy arrays, vectorization, and plotting
text:
8. Market demand from individual buyers
Where does a smooth demand curve come from? Suppose 90 buyers each want one unit and each has a willingness to pay (WTP). At price \(P\), quantity demanded is the number of buyers whose WTP is at least \(P\).
We draw WTPs at random from a uniform distribution between 0 and 60. The seed makes the “random” draws the same every time the notebook runs, so your results can be reproduced.

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=431)
wtp = rng.uniform(0, 60, size=90)
print(np.round(np.sort(wtp)[:8], 1), "...")

print("Demand at P = 30:", (wtp >= 30).sum())

[0.8 1.2 1.3 1.7 2.  2.1 3.5 4.6] ...
Demand at P = 30: 49


For a whole price grid, compare every buyer with every price. wtp[:, None] turns the 90 WTPs into a column, so comparing it with the row of prices gives a 90 × 200 table of True/False values (this is called broadcasting). Summing down each column counts the buyers at each price.

buys = wtp[:, None] >= p_plot     # shape (90 buyers, 200 prices)
print(buys.shape)
q_sim = buys.sum(axis=0)          # count buyers at each price

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.step(q_sim, p_plot, where="post", label="90 simulated buyers")
ax.plot(demand(p_plot, a, b), p_plot, "--", label="Linear demand, a = 90, b = 1.5")
ax.set_xlabel("Quantity")
ax.set_ylabel("Price")
ax.set_title("Individual choices add up to a demand curve")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

(90, 200)









With WTP uniform on \([0, 60]\), the expected share of buyers with WTP above \(P\) is \(1 - P/60\), so 90 buyers give expected demand \(90 - 1.5P\), the curve we’ve used all week. The simulated curve has steps because each buyer is one unit, and it wanders around the line because of the random draws. More buyers make it smoother (Lab 3). Week 15’s agent-based models start from exactly this idea.

2. One variable: its distribution
How unequal are countries’ incomes today? A histogram counts countries in bins of income:

fig.tight_layout()

In logs, the shape is closer to symmetric, because the gap between $2,000 and $4,000 matters about as much as the gap between $20,000 and $40,000: equal ratios are equal distances. The 90th-percentile country is many times richer than the 10th-percentile country.

section: 3. A variable over time, and why logs
text:
3. A variable over time, and why logs
A straight line on a log scale is a constant growth rate. Compare the same US series on both scales, with a dashed line showing constant 2% annual growth from 1850:

usa = mpd[(mpd["countrycode"] == "USA") & (mpd["year"] >= 1850)].sort_values("year")
g_avg = (np.log(usa["gdppc"].iloc[-1]) - np.log(usa["gdppc"].iloc[0])) / (usa["year"].iloc[-1] - usa["year"].iloc[0])
two_pct = usa["gdppc"].iloc[0] * 1.02 ** (usa["year"] - 1850)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
for ax, scale in zip(axes, ["linear", "log"]):
    ax.plot(usa["year"], usa["gdppc"], label="US GDP per capita")
    ax.plot(usa["year"], two_pct, "--", color="gray", label="2% a year from 1850")
    ax.set_yscale(scale)
    ax.set_xlabel("Year")
    ax.set_title(f"{scale.capitalize()} scale")
axes[0].set_ylabel("GDP per capita (2011 intl. $)")
axes[0].legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"average growth 1850-2018: {100 * g_avg:.2f}% a year")








average growth 1850-2018: 1.62% a year


On the linear scale the curve looks like it takes off around 1950, even though growth was steady. On the log scale the US series stays close to a straight line, a little flatter than the 2% reference line (the cell prints the average, about 1.6% a year): its long-run growth rate barely changed, and the dips (the early 1930s, the 1940s) stand out. Use a log scale whenever rates of change are the story, and label the axis so the reader knows.

4. Comparing several series
Many lines need two decisions: put the lines on a log scale if you care about growth, and label the lines directly so the reader doesn’t have to match colors to a legend. Choose readable tick labels:

title: Week 5: Exploratory data analysis and visualization
text:
6. Two variables: a scatter plot
Do poorer countries grow faster? In 1990, countries varied in income. If poor countries catch up, those with low 1990 income should show higher growth from 1990 to 2018. Each point is a country; both axes use logs (growth is already a log difference).

w = mpd.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc")
conv = pd.DataFrame({"log_y1990": np.log(w.loc[1990]),
                     "growth": (np.log(w.loc[2018]) - np.log(w.loc[1990])) / 28 * 100}).dropna()

slope, intercept = np.polyfit(conv["log_y1990"], conv["growth"], 1)
r = np.corrcoef(conv["log_y1990"], conv["growth"])[0, 1]
print(f"{len(conv)} countries; slope {slope:.2f} percentage points per unit of log income; correlation {r:.2f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
ax.scatter(conv["log_y1990"], conv["growth"], s=18, alpha=0.7)
xs = np.linspace(conv["log_y1990"].min(), conv["log_y1990"].max(), 50)
ax.plot(xs, intercept + slope * xs, color="black", linewidth=1.5, label="fitted line")
for name in ["China", "India", "United States", "Qatar", "Japan"]:
    ax.annotate(name, (conv.loc[name, "log_y1990"], conv.loc[name, "growth"]), fontsize=8,
                xytext=(4, 4), textcoords="offset points")
ax.axhline(0, color="gray", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("log GDP per capita, 1990")
ax.set_ylabel("Average annual growth, 1990-2018 (%)")
ax.set_title("Initial income and later growth, 1990-2018")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

169 countries; slope -0.02 percentage points per unit of log income; correlation -0.01









The fitted line is almost flat: across all 169 countries, 1990 income says essentially nothing about growth over the next 28 years. That is not what a simple “poor countries catch up” story predicts. It does not rule out catching up among countries that are alike in other ways, which is what economists usually test, with regression (Week 14). A fitted line is a summary of the pattern, not a law, and a different window or sample can change it. Notice how much the result depends on which of the 169 rows you include.

section: 8. Making a figure someone else will read
text:
8. Making a figure someone else will read
Everything from Week 3’s checklist still applies. For figures with data, add:

Say what the axis is: units, and “log scale” if it is.
Show the source, on the figure or in a caption.
Label lines directly when there are more than three or four.
Show the data points when there are few of them.
Make the title the finding, and check that the figure supports it.
Choose the figure for the question: distribution (histogram), change over time (line), comparison across groups (points or bars), relationship (scatter).


Stating the finding
A finding is a sentence with a number in it, the evidence, and a caveat. You can build it from variables, so the text always matches the computation:

d = conv["growth"]
display(Markdown(
    f"**Finding.** Between 1990 and 2018 the median country's GDP per capita grew {d.median():.1f}% a year "
    f"({len(conv)} countries), and the fitted line of growth on 1990 income has a slope of {slope:.2f}. "
    f"*Caveat:* the line is nearly flat (correlation {r:.2f}), so 1990 income does not predict growth in this sample; it says nothing about catching up among similar countries."
))

Finding. Between 1990 and 2018 the median country’s GDP per capita grew 2.2% a year (169 countries), and the fitted line of growth on 1990 income has a slope of -0.02. Caveat: the line is nearly flat (correlation -0.01), so 1990 income does not predict growth in this sample; it says nothing about catching up among similar countries.

title: Week 7: Linear algebra and Markov chains
text:
Open in Colab · View on GitHub
Many economic models are, at heart, a system of linear equations: markets that affect each other, industries that buy from each other, and states that an economy moves between. Last week’s solvers handle one equation at a time; this week you solve many at once, and you study a model that moves through time by chance, a Markov chain.
After this week you can:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

title: Week 7: Linear algebra and Markov chains
text:
1. Vectors, matrices, and @
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, a vector a single column. The operator @ is matrix multiplication; * multiplies element by element, which is not the same thing.

M = np.array([[2.0, 1.0],
              [1.0, 3.0]])
x = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
print("M @ x =", M @ x)
print("M * x =", M * x)        # elementwise: each column scaled, not a matrix product
print("shape of M:", M.shape, "  transpose:\n", M.T)

M @ x = [4. 7.]
M * x = [[2. 2.]
 [1. 6.]]
shape of M: (2, 2)   transpose:
 [[2. 1.]
 [1. 3.]]

title: Week 7: Linear algebra and Markov chains
text:
2. Solving \(Mx = b\)
Three related markets have prices \(p_1, p_2, p_3\). In market \(i\) demand is \(a_i - \sum_j b_{ij}\,p_j\) (own price matters most; the others are substitutes, so a higher price elsewhere raises demand here), and supply is \(c_i + d_i\,p_i\). Setting demand equal to supply in all three markets gives
\[(B + D)\,p = a - c,\]
a linear system. np.linalg.solve finds the prices in one step.

B = np.array([[ 4.0, -1.0, -0.5],
              [-1.0,  3.5, -1.0],
              [-0.5, -1.0,  3.0]])
D = np.diag([2.0, 3.0, 2.5])          # supply slopes
a = np.array([100.0, 80.0, 60.0])
c = np.array([10.0, 5.0, 0.0])

p = np.linalg.solve(B + D, a - c)
print("equilibrium prices:", p.round(3))
print("largest residual:", np.abs((B + D) @ p - (a - c)).max())

equilibrium prices: [19.127 16.9   15.721]
largest residual: 1.4210854715202004e-14


What if the demand intercept in market 2 shifts? The inverse matrix \((B+D)^{-1}\) holds every cross-effect at once: column \(j\) says how all prices respond to a one-unit shift in market \(j\)’s intercept. Computing it is fine for a small matrix we want to read; to solve a single system, solve is faster and more accurate.

M = np.linalg.inv(B + D)
print(M.round(3))
shock = np.array([0.0, 10.0, 0.0])
print("price changes after +10 on market 2's intercept:", (M @ shock).round(3))
print("check by re-solving:", (np.linalg.solve(B + D, a + shock - c) - p).round(3))

[[0.173 0.03  0.021]
 [0.03  0.163 0.032]
 [0.021 0.032 0.19 ]]
price changes after +10 on market 2's intercept: [0.299 1.634 0.324]
check by re-solving: [0.299 1.634 0.324]


A shock to market 2 raises price 2 the most (by about 1.6) and spills over to markets 1 and 3 (by 0.3 each), exactly as the off-diagonal entries of the inverse say.

title: Week 7: Linear algebra and Markov chains
text:
3. Input-output: the Leontief model
Three industries each use the others’ output. Let \(A_{ij}\) be the amount of industry \(i\)’s output needed to make one unit of industry \(j\)’s output, and \(d\) the final demand. Total output \(x\) must cover what industries use plus final demand:
\[x = Ax + d \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (I - A)\,x = d.\]
The matrix \(L = (I-A)^{-1}\) is the Leontief inverse: column \(j\) gives the total output (direct and indirect) needed across all industries for one unit of final demand for \(j\).

A_io = np.array([[0.20, 0.10, 0.05],
                 [0.30, 0.25, 0.15],
                 [0.10, 0.20, 0.10]])
d = np.array([50.0, 100.0, 150.0])

x = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(3) - A_io, d)
print("total output:", x.round(2))
L = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(3) - A_io)
print("column sums of Leontief inverse (output multipliers):", L.sum(axis=0).round(3))

total output: [104.26 220.49 227.25]
column sums of Leontief inverse (output multipliers): [2.215 2.049 1.576]


Another way to get the same answer. Production happens in rounds: first make \(d\), then the inputs for \(d\), then the inputs for those, and so on, so \(x = d + Ad + A^2 d + \cdots\). Iterating \(x \leftarrow Ax + d\) converges to the same \(x\).

xi = np.zeros(3)
for n in range(1, 500):
    xn = A_io @ xi + d
    if np.abs(xn - xi).max() < 1e-10:
        break
    xi = xn
print(f"converged after {n} rounds:", xn.round(2))
print("same as solve:", np.allclose(xn, x))

converged after 40 rounds: [104.26 220.49 227.25]
same as solve: True

title: Week 7: Linear algebra and Markov chains
section: 4. When a linear system is fragile
text:
4. When a linear system is fragile
Some systems are almost unsolvable: two equations nearly the same line. The condition number measures this; a large one means tiny changes in \(b\) cause large changes in the answer.

M2 = np.array([[1.0, 1.0],
               [1.0, 1.0001]])
print("condition number:", round(np.linalg.cond(M2)))
print("solution for b = (2, 2.0001):", np.linalg.solve(M2, [2.0, 2.0001]))
print("solution for b = (2, 2.0002):", np.linalg.solve(M2, [2.0, 2.0002]))
print("condition number of the market system:", round(np.linalg.cond(B + D), 2))

condition number: 40002
solution for b = (2, 2.0001): [1. 1.]
solution for b = (2, 2.0002): [0. 2.]
condition number of the market system: 1.73


Changing one entry of \(b\) by 0.0001 moved the solution from \((1, 1)\) to \((0, 2)\): with a condition number near 40,000, you lose about four or five digits of accuracy. The market system, at about 1.7, is perfectly safe. If you estimate a model and the condition number of your matrix is huge (collinear regressors, for instance), distrust the coefficients.

title: Week 7: Linear algebra and Markov chains
text:
5. Markov chains
A Markov chain describes something that moves between a few states, where the chance of the next state depends only on the current state. Collect the probabilities in a matrix \(P\) with \(P_{ij} = \Pr(\text{next} = j \mid \text{now} = i)\); each row sums to 1. If \(\pi_t\) is the row vector of probabilities over states at time \(t\), then \(\pi_{t+1} = \pi_t P\), so \(\pi_{t+n} = \pi_t P^n\).
Our states: expansion (0) or recession (1), using the NBER’s dated recessions for the quarterly US data from Week 5.

from pathlib import Path
DATA = "../data" if Path("../data").exists() else "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WSU-EconS431/site/main/data"
us = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA}/us_macro_1959_2009.csv")
us["q"] = pd.PeriodIndex.from_fields(year=us["year"], quarter=us["quarter"], freq="Q")
us = us.set_index("q")
rec = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA}/nber_recessions.csv")

in_rec = pd.Series(0, index=us.index)
for r in rec.itertuples():
    in_rec.loc[pd.Period(r.peak_quarter):pd.Period(r.trough_quarter)] = 1
s = in_rec.to_numpy()
print(f"{len(s)} quarters, {s.sum()} of them in recession ({s.mean():.1%})")

203 quarters, 38 of them in recession (18.7%)


Estimating \(P\). Count the transitions from each state to each state, then divide each row by its total.

counts = np.zeros((2, 2))
for now, nxt in zip(s[:-1], s[1:]):
    counts[now, nxt] += 1
P = counts / counts.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
print("counts:\n", counts)
print("P =\n", P.round(3))

counts:
 [[156.   8.]
 [  8.  30.]]
P =
 [[0.951 0.049]
 [0.211 0.789]]


Expansions are persistent (95% stay expansions), and recessions are too, though much less (79% stay recessions). Two numbers follow directly. The chance of leaving a state each quarter is \(1 - P_{ii}\), so the expected duration is \(1/(1-P_{ii})\):

print(f"expected expansion length: {1 / (1 - P[0, 0]):.1f} quarters")
print(f"expected recession length: {1 / (1 - P[1, 1]):.1f} quarters")

expected expansion length: 20.5 quarters
expected recession length: 4.8 quarters


Where does the chain end up? Start anywhere and apply \(P\) many times: the distribution settles to a stationary distribution \(\pi^*\) with \(\pi^* = \pi^* P\). That is, \(\pi^*\) is a left eigenvector of \(P\) with eigenvalue 1. Two ways to find it:

# (1) eigenvector of P transposed
w, v = np.linalg.eig(P.T)
pi_star = np.real(v[:, np.argmax(np.real(w))])
pi_star = pi_star / pi_star.sum()
print("eigenvector method:", pi_star.round(4))

# (2) just iterate
dist = np.array([0.0, 1.0])          # start in recession
for n in range(200):
    dist = dist @ P
print("after 200 steps from recession:", dist.round(4))
print("share of quarters actually in recession:", s.mean().round(4))

eigenvector method: [0.8119 0.1881]
after 200 steps from recession: [0.8119 0.1881]
share of quarters actually in recession: 0.1872


The chain’s long-run recession share (about 19%) matches the sample share, as it should: the transition counts come from the same data. How fast it forgets its starting point is governed by the second eigenvalue of \(P\) (here about 0.74): each quarter, the gap to \(\pi^*\) shrinks by about that factor.

dist = np.array([0.0, 1.0])
gaps = []
for n in range(15):
    gaps.append(abs(dist[1] - pi_star[1]))
    dist = dist @ P
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.semilogy(gaps, "o-")
ax.set_xlabel("quarters after starting in recession")
ax.set_ylabel("gap between P(recession) and long-run share")
ax.set_title("A Markov chain forgets where it started")
plt.show()
print("second eigenvalue:", np.sort(np.real(w))[0].round(3))

6. A second chain: high or low unemployment
Define the state as high unemployment (6% or more) or low, using the same quarterly data. High unemployment is very persistent here, which changes the long-run answer.

st = (us["unemp"].to_numpy() >= 6.0).astype(int)
C = np.zeros((2, 2))
for now, nxt in zip(st[:-1], st[1:]):
    C[now, nxt] += 1
P2 = C / C.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
print("P2 =\n", P2.round(3))

# stationary distribution by solving (P' - I) pi = 0 with the extra equation sum(pi) = 1
M3 = np.vstack([P2.T - np.eye(2), np.ones(2)])
pi2 = np.linalg.lstsq(M3, np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]), rcond=None)[0]
print("stationary distribution:", pi2.round(3), "  share of sample quarters in high-unemployment:", st.mean().round(3))
print("expected high-unemployment spell:", round(1 / (1 - P2[1, 1]), 1), "quarters")

P2 =
 [[0.944 0.056]
 [0.079 0.921]]
stationary distribution: [0.587 0.413]   share of sample quarters in high-unemployment: 0.379
expected high-unemployment spell: 12.7 quarters


The stationary share (about 41%) differs from the sample share (about 38%): the chain is estimated from transitions only, and the sample is a short, specific stretch of history. Always ask whether the “long run” of a model describes the data’s own history or something the data did not live long enough to show.
